lead: Mutual information measures how much one random variable tells you about another. In a communication link, the input X is the message symbol and the output Y is what the receiver sees. The channel adds uncertainty, so Y is an imperfect copy of X. Mutual information I(X;Y) is the part of H(X) that the output removes. Engineers use it to compare channels, predict achievable rates, and see why a noisy channel cannot carry unlimited data. It is the quantity that channel capacity maximises, and the basis for error-control coding.
prereq: You need: entropy from entropy and information rate and conditional probability (see the probability and random variables review).

blocks.text: Take two discrete random variables X and Y. X has alphabet {x₁, …, x<sub>M</sub>} and Y has alphabet {y₁, …, y<sub>N</sub>}. The joint entropy H(X,Y) is the average uncertainty of the pair:

blocks.where: P(x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>) is the probability that X=x<sub>i</sub> and Y=y<sub>j</sub>; the sum runs over all pairs; entropy is in bits when log₂ is used.

blocks.text: Conditional entropy H(X|Y) is the uncertainty left in X after Y is known:

blocks.where: P(x<sub>i</sub>|y<sub>j</sub>) is the conditional probability of x<sub>i</sub> given y<sub>j</sub>. H(Y|X) is defined the same way with the roles swapped.

blocks.text: Both formulas use the convention 0 log₂ 0 = 0, so terms with zero probability contribute nothing to the sum. A channel matrix with zero entries therefore causes no trouble.
The chain rule splits the joint uncertainty:

blocks.where: H(X) is the source entropy from Chapter 7.1. The rule says: first learn X, then learn the extra uncertainty in Y given X. Order does not change the total. In general H(X|Y) ≠ H(Y|X). The first asks how much uncertainty about the input remains after the output; the second asks how much uncertainty about the output remains after the input. They are equal only in special symmetric cases.

blocks.text: Mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty:

I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X)
       = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y)
blocks.where: I(X;Y) is mutual information in bits, H(X) and H(Y) are source and output entropies, and H(X|Y), H(Y|X) are conditional entropies. The three forms are equivalent by the chain rule.

blocks.text: I(X;Y) is symmetric: I(X;Y)=I(Y;X). It measures shared uncertainty, not direction. It cannot be negative, because conditioning cannot increase average uncertainty. It cannot exceed either entropy: 0 ≤ I(X;Y) ≤ min(H(X), H(Y)). If X and Y are independent, I=0. If Y is a deterministic function of X, I=H(Y) and H(Y|X)=0. If X is a deterministic function of Y, I=H(X) and H(X|Y)=0.

Picture H(X) and H(Y) as two overlapping regions. The overlap is I(X;Y); the part of H(X) outside it is H(X|Y), also called the equivocation, and the part of H(Y) outside it is H(Y|X). Because I is a part of H(X), it can never be larger than H(X). Some syllabi call I(X;Y) the average mutual information.

A discrete memoryless channel (DMC) has input alphabet X, output alphabet Y, and transition probabilities P(y<sub>j</sub>|x<sub>i</sub>). The channel matrix has rows for inputs and columns for outputs:

blocks.where: row i gives the output distribution when input x<sub>i</sub> is sent, so every row sums to 1. Memoryless means each output Y<sub>k</sub> depends only on the input X<sub>k</sub> at that instant, not on earlier inputs or outputs.

blocks.text: For a binary symmetric channel (BSC), input and output are {0,1}. With crossover probability p, a sent bit flips with probability p and is correct with probability 1−p. The channel matrix is [[1−p, p],[p, 1−p]]. Given the input, the output uncertainty is the binary entropy:

blocks.where: p is the crossover probability and H(p) is in bits. Then
H(Y) depends on the input distribution P(X). For equiprobable input, H(Y)=1 bit because the BSC is symmetric, so I=1−H(p).

blocks.text: A binary erasure channel passes the bit correctly with probability 1−e and outputs an erasure symbol with probability e; its capacity is 1−e bits per channel use, reached with equiprobable input. If the channel carries r<sub>s</sub> symbols per second, the information rate is R = r<sub>s</sub> I(X;Y) bits/s.

figure.caption: The binary symmetric channel of the worked examples flips a bit with p = 0.1. Of the output entropy, 0.469 bit is noise whatever is sent; the rest is mutual information: 0.531 bit with equally likely inputs, only 0.456 bit when 0 is sent 70 % of the time.

examples.question: A binary symmetric channel has crossover probability p = 0.1. The input symbols 0 and 1 are equally likely. The channel is used at r<sub>s</sub> = 1000 symbols per second. Find H(X), H(Y|X), H(Y), I(X;Y) and the information rate R. Give entropies in bits per symbol and R in bit/s.
steps: Input distribution: P(0)=P(1)=0.5. H(X)=−0.5 log₂0.5 −0.5 log₂0.5 = 1 bit/symbol.
The BSC is symmetric and the input is equiprobable, so P(Y=0)=P(Y=1)=0.5. Thus H(Y)=1 bit/symbol.
examples.answer: H(X)=1 bit/symbol, H(Y|X)=0.469 bits/symbol, H(Y)=1 bit/symbol, I(X;Y)=0.531 bits/symbol and R=531 bit/s.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.1
rs = 1000
HX = 1.0
HYX = -(p * math.log2(p) + (1 - p) * math.log2(1 - p))
HY = 1.0
I = HY - HYX
R = rs * I
print(round(HX, 3))
print(round(HYX, 3))
print(round(HY, 3))
print(round(I, 3))
print(round(R, 3))

examples.question: The same BSC (p = 0.1) is driven with P(X = 0) = 0.7 and P(X = 1) = 0.3. Find P(Y = 0), H(Y), I(X;Y) and H(X|Y), and compare I with worked example 1.
steps: H(Y|X) = H(0.1) = 0.469 bits, whatever the input probabilities, because each row of the channel matrix is the same pair 0.9, 0.1.

Check with the other form: H(X) = H(0.7) = 0.8813 bits; the joint table gives H(X,Y) = 1.3503 bits, so H(X|Y) = H(X,Y) − H(Y) = 1.3503 − 0.9248 = 0.4255 bits and H(X) − H(X|Y) = 0.8813 − 0.4255 = 0.4558 bits. The two forms agree.
Comparison: 0.4558 < 0.531 bits. The unequal input wastes part of the channel; the equal input of worked example 1 is the best one, which is why chapter 7.4 calls 0.531 bits the capacity.
examples.answer: P(Y = 0) = 0.66, H(Y) = 0.925 bits, I(X;Y) = 0.456 bits/symbol and H(X|Y) = 0.426 bits; the equally likely input gives more (0.531 bits).

traps: Swapping H(X|Y) and H(Y|X). They answer different questions and are not generally equal; only symmetric cases make them equal.
Claiming I(X;Y) can be larger than H(X) or H(Y). The overlap cannot be larger than either region; 0 ≤ I ≤ min(H(X),H(Y)).

Writing I = H(X) + H(Y) + H(X,Y). H(X) + H(Y) counts the overlap twice; subtracting H(X,Y), which counts it once, leaves the overlap alone. With the plus sign the result is larger than H(X,Y) itself, so it cannot be a shared part.
Reading a channel matrix row as an output distribution that must sum with other rows. Each row is conditional on one input and sums to 1; columns need not sum to 1.
For a BSC, plugging p into I directly. The input-dependent term is H(Y); the fixed noise term is H(p).

quiz.q: Define mutual information I(X;Y) and state two equivalent formulas.
quiz.a: I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X|Y)=H(Y)−H(Y|X). It is the average uncertainty about X removed by observing Y.

quiz.q: Why must I(X;Y) lie between 0 and min(H(X),H(Y))?
quiz.a: Conditioning cannot increase average entropy, so H(X|Y)≥0 gives I≤H(X); symmetry gives I≤H(Y). Mutual information is an average of non-negative information terms, so I≥0.

quiz.q: A BSC has p=0.2 and equiprobable input. Find H(Y|X), H(Y), I(X;Y), in bits/symbol.
A channel maps both inputs 0 and 1 to output 0 always. Find I(X;Y). Explain using H(X|Y) and H(Y).
quiz.a: Y is constant, H(Y)=0; I=H(Y)−H(Y|X)=0. Equivalently, seeing Y gives no information about X, so H(X|Y)=H(X) and I=0.

quiz.q: What does memoryless mean for a DMC?
quiz.a: Each output Y<sub>k</sub> depends only on the input X<sub>k</sub> at the same time, not on past inputs or outputs.

quiz.q: In a DMC, H(X)=1.2 bits and H(X|Y)=0.3 bits. Find I(X;Y). Can you also find H(Y|X) from these data?
quiz.a: I=1.2−0.3=0.9 bits. H(Y|X) cannot be found because H(Y) is not given; I=H(Y)−H(Y|X) has two unknowns.

quiz.q: For a BSC with p=0.5, find I(X;Y) for any input distribution. Explain.
quiz.a: H(Y|X)=H(0.5)=1 bit. Output is independent of input because each output is equally likely 0 or 1 regardless of input, so H(Y)=1 and I=1−1=0. A completely random channel carries no information.

beyond: Not for the exam. Mutual information is used in modern channel codes, including LDPC and polar codes, to track how many bits survive after each decoding step. It also appears in machine learning as a feature-selection score and in 5G link adaptation. Search for “mutual information channel capacity”, “binary symmetric channel mutual information” and “EXIT chart mutual information” to go further.
